defs_parts: Five labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
Video only: the term comes from a video lecture, and is not in the course text or on the term list.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: Descriptive play shows a response, and evaluative play asks why it matters.
Risk versus reward pays more for the harder, riskier action.
A trade-off is one swap, and persistence makes a choice stick for a set time.
Situational choice depends on the moment, personalisation on the player's style.
Difficulty is how hard it is, and fairness is whether you can learn from losing.
Rock-paper-scissors keeps options balanced, and short turns keep downtime low.
bookends.command: Quiz me on game design terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use descriptive play, evaluative play, agency, risk versus reward, trade-off, persistence, situational choice, personalisation, difficulty and fairness. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

beats.narration_text: Building Virtual Environments, Exam Prep. Key Terms: Choices and Challenge. Nineteen terms about game design, from meaningful play and agency to risk, trade-offs, fairness, luck, balance and downtime. With the exact term you can tell a playtester, or an AI coding agent, what to change.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say a hard game is an unfair game. It is not. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is. Fairness is whether the player can learn from losing. A game can be very hard and still fair. This film goes through nineteen terms on choices and challenge, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

beats.narration_text: A red bola flies across and hits a block of ice, and the ice shatters. Meaningful play means the player acts and the game responds in a way that matters. Descriptive play is the first half of that, an action followed by a clear response the player sees at once. For example, in a platformer you build, the player stomps an enemy, it flattens with a squash sound, and the way ahead is clear.

beats.narration_text: Two lines branch through three forks. Agency, also called autonomy, means the player takes control of how the game is played. Three forks with two ways each make eight possible routes, two times two times two, and the red player and the black player finish the same level by different ones. For example, give your level a high path over the spikes and a low path under them, and let each player decide which way to go.

beats.narration_text: Bars of points. Risk versus reward means a harder or riskier action pays more, and the player weighs the factors before trying it. In this made-up example an invader is worth ten to thirty points, while the UFO, which is harder to hit, gives fifty to one hundred fifty, and three hundred on the twenty-third shot. For example, put a coin on a narrow ledge right above the spikes and make it worth more than the coins on the safe path.

beats.narration_text: Three situations, each scored as reward minus cost. A Meaningful choice changes what happens, and the player has to think about it. In this made-up example the same UFO scores plus twenty-five point five when the player is behind, minus seventeen when the invaders are near, and plus three on the last life. For example, a player on one heart has to think hard about jumping for a bonus coin over a pit, while a player on full health may simply go for it.

beats.narration_text: A score line over time. A Trade-off means giving up one thing to get another. In this made-up example the grey player scores a steady ten points a second. The red player gives up a ship at eight seconds, rescues it for dual fire, then scores twenty a second, and pulls ahead after eighteen seconds. For example, offer the player a heavy shield that blocks every hit but makes them jump lower.

beats.narration_text: Eight moments in a stage, and four power pellets. Persistence means the player has to carry the consequences of a choice for a set time. Here all four pellets go on the first four moments, the red boxes, so at the big group of ghosts none are left until the next stage. For example, if the player spends all of the level's bombs on the first few enemies, the boss at the end has to be fought without them.

beats.narration_text: A grid of enemies, sorted by how they move and how they attack. Unit differentiation, also called orthogonal unit differentiation, means each enemy type does something different, which forces the player to prioritise. The imp charges and its fireballs can be dodged, the cacodemon stays back, and the shotgun guy never misses. For example, give your platformer one enemy that rushes the player along a ledge and another that throws rocks from far away.

beats.narration_text: Bars now rank the threat you cannot dodge. Situational choice means the same choice is better or worse depending on the situation the player is in. In this made-up example the shotgun guy deals ten damage a second that cannot be dodged, the cacodemon three, and the imp two point five, so the shotgun guy goes first. For example, with a turret and a walking enemy in the room, break the turret first, but with walkers alone, jumping over them may be better.

beats.narration_text: Three rows of decisions, red for a risky pick and black for a safe one. Personalisation means players build their own play style from the decisions they make. All three face the same twenty decisions, and each chooses a different mix. For example, in a level with an optional enemy in every room, one player fights each one while another sneaks past them all, and both reach the goal.

beats.narration_text: Now each row is counted, in this simulated run. The aggressive player took the risky pick sixteen times out of twenty, eighty percent. The mixed player, eleven, fifty-five percent. The cautious player, three, fifteen percent. That spread of styles is personalisation. For example, the playtest notes for your platformer might show one tester always taking the spike path for the bonus coins, and another never taking it.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Descriptive play shows a response, and evaluative play asks why it matters. Risk versus reward pays more for the harder, riskier action. A trade-off is one swap, and persistence makes a choice stick for a set time. Situational choice depends on the moment, personalisation on the player's style. Difficulty is how hard it is, and fairness is whether you can learn from losing. Rock-paper-scissors keeps options balanced, and short turns keep downtime low.
